newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Sentencing postponed in HK Carrian case.
newsitem.headline: Sentencing postponed in HK Carrian case.

text.p: The judge presiding over Hong Kong's biggest corporate fraud trial delayed sentencing disgraced tycoon George Tan on Monday and made no order on costs.

"How can I rubber stamp an agreement you have made with the prosecution...when the taxpayer has spent all these millions... because Mr Tan did not want to plead guilty until last week," judge Michael Stuart-Moore told defence lawyers in court.
The wrangle sent the 13-year-long case back into a state of suspense which had earlier appeared to end when Tan pleaded guilty last Friday to two counts of conspiracy to defraud.
The charges he admitted to were linked to HK$1.8 billion (US$238 million) in secret loans from the Malaysian bank, Bumiputra Malaysia Finance Ltd, in the 1980s.
A further 11 charges were dropped as part of a plea bargain between prosecutors and defence to avoid further expense.
Prosecutors revealed in court on Monday that the inquiry into the case and Tan's trial had cost the authorities over HK$200 million (US$25.6 million) in taxpayers' money.

Defence lawyer Anthony Scrivener pleaded for mitigation at the sentencing hearing by arguing that Tan, 62, had not actually swindled the bank but had simply taken a risk with its money. The lawyer also drew attention to Tan's poor health.
"It's not alleged that Tan has stolen anything," Scrivener said, pointing out that the case had dragged on for 11 years and that Tan had respected bail for 13 years.
Prosecutor Martin Wilson said the plea bargain included an agreement not to apply for costs to avoid spending millions more on the trial and added that Tan might not be able to pay in any case.
The judge decided to postpone his sentencing until Friday, saying: "I have a lot to think about."
Tan was once helmsman of one of Hong Kong's biggest business empires, but he was a broken man as he appeared in court.
Doctors testified to his dementia, paranoia and depression. Since his fall Tan has had a heart attack and a stroke and walks with a limp.
Tan and his Carrian group stormed on to the scene with spectacular property deals that made Carrian one of the most successful business empires in Hong Kong's history.

The Carrian group had diverse interests including a property, shipping and restaurant empire. By the end of 1981, it was the seventh largest company in Hong Kong. Its 1983 collapse under a mountain of debt was the territory's biggest.
Even if the Carrian case is closed, mystery surrounds what was one of the biggest corporate scandals in Asian history.

An investigator sent from Malaysia to Hong Kong to probe the scandal was found strangled in a banana grove near the Chinese border, and another figure linked to the case was found dead at the bottom of a swimming pool.
